initial.source:
# This script puts everything in the normal output channel. Repair the destinations.
printf 'Destination: %s\n' "$1"
printf 'Queued: %s\n' "$1"
printf 'Done\n'

teaching.prerequisite_note: Builds on quoted arguments, printf, file replacement and error output from the foundations unit.

concepts.title: Choose where text goes
concepts.text: Normal output is the result a caller may use. Standard error is a separate channel for notices and problems. A message can be useful without belonging in a saved report.

concepts.title: Redirection changes a destination
concepts.text: > sends normal output to a file and replaces its contents. >&2 sends normal output to the problem channel. 2> captures text a command already writes to that problem channel. Each redirection applies to its own command.

concepts.title: A command error is not broken syntax
concepts.text: In this example cat cannot find a sample file. Its exit status 1 is expected; its problem message is saved to notes.txt. The script itself is readable. Compare the output display with the resulting simulated file.

teaching.inputs: Argument 1 is unavailable.txt, which does not exist; argument 2 is notes.txt. The keep file must stay unchanged.
teaching.try_change: Change 2> to >, then run again. Which destination now receives the problem message?

after./work/notes.txt: cat: unavailable.txt: No such file or directory

scenarios.retry_guidance: Compare the report file, normal output and problem output separately. A correct message in the wrong destination still changes how another program would use the script.
scenarios.explanation: The report is a file result, Done is normal output, and Queued is a separate notice. Redirect each printf independently. Replacing the slip prevents old content from leaking into the result; other files are part of the checks too.

scenarios.summary: Build a pipeline that keeps the right severity and component, with an honest exit status.

Print only lines containing both ERROR and the component text, in their original order, each ending in a newline. Print no headings or problem messages and change no files. Return 0 when any line matches and 1 when none match. Matching is case-sensitive substring matching, not a regular expression.

teaching.prerequisite_note: Builds on literal grep, quoted arguments, output channels and status.

concepts.title: A pipe connects two commands
concepts.text: The | symbol sends the normal output of the command on its left into the input of the command on its right. Only the lines surviving the first filter can reach the second filter.

concepts.title: Two filters form an intersection
concepts.text: A line must satisfy both filters to survive. The example first selects OPEN lines, then selects a visitor name. With -F, matching means literal text anywhere in the line; letter case matters.

concepts.title: The last stage reports the pipeline status
concepts.text: In this portable subset, a pipeline returns its last command’s exit status. grep returns 0 for matches and 1 for no matches. That says nothing by itself about whether an earlier command could read a file; this assignment supplies existing files.

teaching.inputs: Arguments are visitors.txt and Mina. The file contains OPEN Rowan, CLOSED Mina and OPEN Mina on separate lines.
teaching.try_change: Change OPEN to CLOSED and run again; the second filter should still require Mina.

files./work/visitors.txt:

CLOSED Mina
OPEN Mina

after./work/visitors.txt:

CLOSED Mina

scenarios.retry_guidance: Check both required conditions: a line from another component or a non-ERROR line must not pass. Compare the selected input set before changing the filter.
scenarios.explanation: The two literal conditions form an intersection. Reversing their order is an equally valid solution here because both are pure filters. The final grep provides the requested match/no-match status. A missing input would need a separate guard in a different assignment.

hints: The last read can provide text while reporting that no newline was found.

initial.source:
# A final line without a newline is currently lost. Repair the loop condition.
while read -r line; do
    printf 'Ticket: %s\n' "$line"
done

cases.name: Backslashes and spaces
cases.stdout:
Ticket: C:\jobs  waiting
Ticket: final  tail

cases.name: Unterminated whitespace is empty after trimming

solution:
while read -r line || [ -n "$line" ]; do
    printf 'Ticket: %s\n' "$line"
done

teaching.prerequisite_note: Builds on read -r, tests, printf and exit status. This lesson introduces while and ||.

concepts.title: Repeat while an action succeeds
concepts.text: while runs its do … done body whenever the condition reports status 0. read -r takes the next line each time, so this loop makes progress toward the end of a finite input.

concepts.title: End-of-input is a status, not always an empty value
concepts.text: read reports a nonzero status when it reaches the end before a newline. It can still have stored useful final text in the variable. A complete blank line is different: read succeeds and stores an empty value.

concepts.title: Try another condition after failure
concepts.text: A || B runs B only if A fails. The example accepts either a complete read or a non-empty final value. Once both fail, the loop ends; with no input it does no work.

teaching.example:
while read -r name || [ -n "$name" ]; do
    printf 'Visitor: %s\n' "$name"
done
teaching.inputs: Input is Mina followed by a newline, then Rowan without a final newline. No arguments or files are needed.
teaching.try_change: Remove || [ -n "$name" ] and run again. Notice which visitor disappears, then restore the condition.

scenarios.retry_guidance: Inspect whether a missing final line break, a blank complete line, or empty input caused the difference. These are three different input conditions.
scenarios.explanation: read communicates both a value and a status. The extra non-empty test preserves the last partial record, but an empty value with failed read ends the loop. The model uses default read whitespace trimming; preserving outer whitespace with IFS is a later capability.

hints: Keep processing after recording a missing-file message.
Remember whether any missing file occurred, then decide the final status after the loop.
A no-match grep status is normal here. It must not masquerade as a missing-file error.
scenarios.simplifications: Portable shell syntax in the documented bounded subset. Only the declared flat /work text files exist. No external command or host file is used. Input paths are ordinary filenames and never start with a hyphen. This unit does not claim a complete Bash implementation.

initial.source:
# Repair this batch: it stops at the first missing path and hides later work.
for path in "$@"; do
    if [ -f "$path" ]; then
        printf 'File: %s\n' "$path"
        grep -F ERROR "$path"
    else
        printf 'Missing: %s\n' "$path" >&2
        exit 2
    fi
done

cases.name: Multiple readable logs
cases.stdout:
File: north.log
ERROR north timeout
File: south.log
ERROR south retry

cases.name: Missing first file but later file still handled
Quiet file and later missing file
Readable quiet log after an incident
cases.stdout:
File: incident.log
ERROR retry
File: quiet.log

solution:
failed=''
for path in "$@"; do
    if [ -f "$path" ]; then
        printf 'File: %s\n' "$path"
        grep -F ERROR "$path"
    else
        printf 'Missing: %s\n' "$path" >&2
        failed=yes
    fi
done
if [ -n "$failed" ]; then
    exit 2
fi
exit 0

teaching.prerequisite_note: Capstone: combines the previous unit and this unit. There is no new shell syntax to memorize.

concepts.title: Keep working, but remember a problem
concepts.text: Exiting inside a loop stops the whole script, so later files never get inspected. A named variable can remember a problem while the for loop continues; the variable keeps its value after that loop.

concepts.title: Report the batch outcome deliberately
concepts.text: A missing file and a readable file with no ERROR lines are different outcomes. The final exit status should summarize the whole batch, rather than accidentally reuse the last filter’s no-match status. The example below only checks file availability; your assignment adds log filtering.

teaching.example:
found_problem=''
for path in "$@"; do
    if [ -f "$path" ]; then
        printf 'Found: %s\n' "$path"
    else
        printf 'Skipped: %s\n' "$path" >&2
        found_problem=yes
    fi
done
if [ -n "$found_problem" ]; then
    exit 2
fi
teaching.inputs: Arguments are menu.txt and missing.txt. Only menu.txt exists and contains tea.
teaching.try_change: Change found_problem=yes to found_problem='' and run again. The warning still prints, but what happens to the exit status?

scenarios.retry_guidance: Check whether later arguments were skipped, a normal no-match result became a failure, or an earlier missing file was forgotten by the final exit status.
scenarios.explanation: An accumulated problem flag separates per-file work from the final batch outcome. Each readable file is independently useful even when another is missing. A quiet file has no ERROR lines, which is acceptable; the requested final status is driven only by missing files.
